meta.title: Who really said "640K ought to be enough for anybody"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bill Gates is credited with it, but no source exists. The wording first appears in an InfoWorld timeline dated 1 January 1990 — and Gates denies saying it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said '640K ought to be enough for anybody'?
meta.ogDescription: No interview, transcript or contemporary report backs this famous line. Earliest print appearance: InfoWorld, 1 January 1990. Gates: "I never said that statement."

answer.label: Not Bill Gates — an unsourced legend
answer.authorDates: Credited to Bill Gates (b. 1955), Microsoft co-founder — who denies it
answer.sourceLine: No interview, transcript, speech recording or contemporary report has ever been produced for this line. The earliest known print appearance of the famous wording is an InfoWorld timeline dated 1 January 1990, which put it in quotation marks beside Gates’s name with no source; Gates has denied it repeatedly since the 1990s.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — widely repeated, never documented, and denied by the man it is pinned on.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Wonder Years: How the PC Industry Grew Up in the ’80s

source.excerpt: IBM introduces the PC and, with Microsoft, releases DOS (“640K ought to be enough for anyone” — Bill Gates)
trail: 29 April 1985 — an InfoWorld editorial by James E. Fawcette attributes to “William Gates, chairman of Microsoft” a different remark about setting the PC-DOS upper limit at 640K, with no precise reference and not from an interview (Quote Investigator ↗).
14 November 1988 — an InfoWorld article by George Morrow paraphrases the claim that Gates had said 640K was more memory than anyone needed (ADS-L citation list ↗).
1 January 1990 — InfoWorld’s decade timeline prints the modern wording in quotation marks beside Gates’s name, still with no reference (Quote Investigator ↗).

January 1996 — Gates answers a reader in his syndicated column: “I’ve said some stupid things and some wrong things, but not that… There’s never a citation; the quotation just floats like a rumor” (Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: The timeline entry from InfoWorld, 1 January 1990 — the earliest known appearance of the famous phrasing. Note the magazine gives no date, place or source for the alleged remark.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full citation history

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted: the line has no identified author or authored work behind it. Its earliest known printings are magazine texts from 1985 and 1990, both well after 1931 and therefore the property of their publisher — but neither is a source for a Gates utterance, only a repetition of one.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: About Bill Gates
author.metaLine: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder, software developer and philanthropist
author.bio: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 and led it through the era of MS-DOS and Windows, the period in which this quotation is supposedly set. The 640K figure was a real constraint of the IBM PC’s architecture, which is why the line sounds plausible — but Gates has said the opposite was true, that “the industry went through” pain because of that ceiling and that Microsoft kept pushing the limit up. He has called the quotation a rumour that floats without a citation.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in “The Wonder Years: How the PC Industry Grew Up in the ’80s,” InfoWorld, 1 January 1990 — where the line appears in quotation marks beside Bill Gates’s name with no source given. An earlier and differently worded remark was attributed to Gates in James E. Fawcette’s InfoWorld editorial of 29 April 1985. Attribution unverified; Gates denies it.

misattribution.heading: How a line nobody said became famous
misattribution.intro: The quotation is almost always dated to 1981 and set at a computer trade show. No attendee, transcript, recording or contemporary report has ever surfaced — the trail runs backwards through magazine repetition, not forwards from an event.

items.why: The setting is part of the legend, not of any documented record. Wikiquote’s talk page ↗ records years of editors demanding contemporary documentation for the 1981 claim, and none being produced.

items.who: Attributed to “William Gates, chairman of Microsoft”
items.why: An InfoWorld editorial by James E. Fawcette dated 29 April 1985 carried a differently worded remark — that when the upper limit of PC-DOS was set at 640K they thought nobody would ever need that much memory — with no precise reference and not from an interview, per Quote Investigator ↗.

“The Wonder Years: How the PC Industry Grew Up in the ’80s,” InfoWorld, 1 January 1990, placed the now-standard phrasing in quotation marks next to Gates’s name without saying when or where he supposedly said it (ADS-L citation list ↗).

items.who: Books and columns repeating the claim
items.why: Proposed sources turn out to be later works restating the story — Computerworld notes a claim that Steven Levy’s Hackers contained a profane version proved untrue (Computerworld ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Best available verdict: the line is unverified and denied. Gates in January 1996: “I’ve said some stupid things and some wrong things, but not that” — and in 2001, “I never said that statement — I said the opposite of that” (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why this one refuses to die
lead: The 640K ceiling was real. The IBM PC’s architecture reserved memory above 640 kilobytes for system use, and for years that limit shaped what PC software could do. A quip in which the industry’s most visible figure waves it off as plenty is almost too neat — it explains a frustration everyone lived through and supplies a villain at the same time.

But neatness is exactly what should make you suspicious. The quotation is usually dated to a 1981 trade show, yet the first time anything like it reaches print is 1985, and the famous wording does not appear until a magazine timeline published on 1 January 1990. Fred Shapiro, editor of The Yale Book of Quotations, appealed publicly for a source and got roughly a hundred replies — none of them a citation, according to Computerworld ↗.
context.detailsSummary: What Gates has actually said about it
detailsBody: Answering a reader in his syndicated newspaper column in January 1996, Gates wrote: “I’ve said some stupid things and some wrong things, but not that. No one involved in computers would ever say that a certain amount of memory is enough for all time,” adding that he kept bumping into the quotation and that it never came with a citation (Wikiquote, Misattributed ↗).

In a U.S. News & World Report interview dated 20 August 2001 he went further: “Do you realize the pain the industry went through while the IBM PC was limited to 640 K? … I never said that statement — I said the opposite of that.”
context.pull: There’s never a citation; the quotation just floats like a rumor.
